# FuzeFront Adoption Quickstart

This guide is for developers and teams evaluating FuzeFront as a real platform component rather than just reading about the architecture.

## Pick your path

### 1. Developer: run the platform locally

```bash
npm run install:all
npm run db:init
npm run db:seed
npm run demo
```

Then inspect the runtime app registry, the example federated application, health updates, routing, and the integration SDK.

### 2. Platform engineer: run the Kubernetes path

```bash
cd FuzeInfra && make kind-up && cd ..

docker build -t fuzefront/backend:local ./backend
docker build -t fuzefront/frontend:local \
  --build-arg VITE_API_URL=http://fuzefront.dev.local ./frontend

kind load docker-image \
  fuzefront/backend:local \
  fuzefront/frontend:local \
  --name fuzeinfra

helm upgrade --install fuzefront deploy/helm/fuzefront \
  -n fuzefront --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/helm/fuzefront/values-local.yaml
```

### 3. Architecture reviewer: challenge the design

Read `docs/SOFTWARE_FACTORY.md`, then join the public architecture review:

https://github.com/izzywdev/FuzeFront/issues/1015

We specifically want concrete failure modes, security concerns, coupling problems, operational risks, and examples where an existing platform solves the problem better.

### 4. Design partner: bring a real workload

Open a Design Partner issue or start from:

https://github.com/izzywdev/FuzeFront/issues/1016

Useful evaluation cases include:

- a startup operating several products with a small team;
- a platform team standardizing app delivery;
- a software studio repeatedly rebuilding common infrastructure;
- a CTO testing governed AI-assisted delivery;
- an independent founder trying to maximize organizational leverage.

## What success looks like

For each real evaluation we want to capture:

- time to first successful local run;
- time to onboard an existing app;
- what manual work was eliminated;
- what still required custom integration;
- where the abstractions leaked;
- deployment and operational friction;
- security or governance concerns;
- whether a second application becomes materially easier than the first.

## Contribute

Look for issues labeled `good first issue`, `help wanted`, `community`, or `adoption`.

Small fixes are welcome. Documentation, examples, integration adapters, developer-experience improvements, tests, reproducible bug reports, and architecture criticism are all useful contributions.

See `COMMUNITY.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the broader participation model.

# =============================================================================
# Production overlay (Contabo k3s), consumed by the Argo CD `fuzefront` Application.
# Differs from local by: GHCR images, public host + TLS, sealed secret, prod
# Authentik OIDC, Prometheus metrics, pre-created Kafka topics, and node-2
# placement for heavy stateless services.
#
# Node topology (see docs/deployment/CONTABO_DEPLOYMENT.md):
#   node-1 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-1): control-plane + stateful
#           (FuzeInfra Postgres/Redis/Kafka/Chroma live here on local-path).
#   node-2 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-2): heavy stateless compute
#           (litellm/chat/billing). Relabel/rename to match the real join.
# All secrets come from the SealedSecret `fuzefront-secrets` — never inline here.
# =============================================================================
global:
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  # Default placement: none (let the scheduler spread app pods across both nodes).
  # Heavy stateless services pin to node-2 via their own affinity blocks below.
  scheduling:
    nodeSelector: {}
    affinity: {}
    # Tolerate FuzeInfra's durable-node taint.
    #
    # FuzeInfra is tainting its three durable (control-plane/etcd) nodes
    # `fuzeinfra.io/durable=true:NoSchedule` so that application workloads stop
    # landing on them. Measured there on 2026-09-07: 70 and 57 pods on two of the
    # three, 20,585 container restarts, load average 59, and etcd losing
    # heartbeats on the node that was also the raft leader.
    #
    # FuzeFront is explicitly IN SCOPE for those nodes -- it is platform frontend,
    # not a tenant app -- so it must carry the toleration or it gets pushed onto
    # the autoscaled elastic pool, which is reaped on billing boundaries.
    #
    # THIS WILL NOT LOOK BROKEN IF IT IS MISSING. NoSchedule does not evict, so
    # when the taint lands every FuzeFront pod keeps running exactly as before.
    # It breaks at the NEXT restart or rollout, when those pods can no longer be
    # placed back -- a delayed failure that reads as unrelated to the taint. That
    # is why this has to land BEFORE the taint, not after it.
    #
    # TOLERATION IS NOT PLACEMENT. This only makes the durable nodes *eligible*;
    # the scheduler may still choose elastic. Moving specific backend services
    # deliberately ONTO elastic is a separate concern, expressed per-service via
    # nodeSelector/affinity (see PR #910) -- and note the `fuzefront.scheduling`
    # helper resolves per-service over global, so a service that declares its own
    # `tolerations` REPLACES this list rather than adding to it. A service pinned
    # to elastic simply does not need it.
    #
    # Tracked in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#913; the matching FuzeInfra-side tolerations
    # (longhorn, coredns, ARC controller, Argo CD) landed in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#921.
    tolerations:
      - key: fuzeinfra.io/durable
        operator: Equal
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule

# Prometheus scrape annotations on FuzeFront pods. The FuzeInfra Prometheus
# auto-discovers pods carrying prometheus.io/scrape=true (see Phase E). The
# backend exposes /metrics via prom-client; other pods are annotated for when
# their /metrics lands.
observability:
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    path: /metrics

# Fleet policy: only core infra + frontend services stay on the durable/
# control-plane node pool (vmi3383846/vmi3396106); backend/worker pods for an
# individual product move to the autoscaled `elastic` pool instead. Every
# service below reaches its state (Postgres/Redis/Mongo/Kafka) over the
# network in the `fuzeinfra` namespace, not via a local PVC, so this is a
# plain placement change — mirrors FuzeInfra's
# runners/arc/runner-scale-set-values.yaml pattern. `frontend` below is
# deliberately NOT given this block; it is the one service this policy keeps
# on durable.
.elasticPlacement: &elasticPlacement
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: fuzeinfra.io/pool
                operator: In
                values:
                  - elastic
  tolerations:
    - key: fuzeinfra.io/elastic
      operator: Exists
      effect: PreferNoSchedule

# Reference App Onboarding Walkthrough: Zero to Registered Runtime

This guide provides an end-to-end reference walkthrough for taking a minimal standalone web application (React/Vite) and onboarding it into the FuzeFront runtime ecosystem so that it becomes visible, authenticated, and healthy.

---

## 1. Architecture & Sequence Diagram

The following diagram illustrates the lifecycle of a reference application as it registers with the FuzeFront platform, establishes auth/routing assumptions, and reports health heartbeats.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Dev as Developer
    participant RefApp as Standalone App (Vite/React)
    participant RegAPI as FuzeFront Applications Service (/api/apps)
    participant Shell as FuzeFront Host Shell
    participant Runtime as FuzeFront Runtime / Health Monitor

    Note over Dev, RefApp: Phase 1: Build & Package Minimal App
    Dev->>RefApp: Initialize Vite project with standard entry point
    RefApp->>RefApp: Implement registration metadata & health endpoint

    Note over RefApp, RegAPI: Phase 2: Registration Contract
    Dev->>RegAPI: POST /api/apps (Register app manifest & entry points)
    RegAPI--oidc->RefApp: Registration Confirmed & Scoped Token Assigned

    Note over Shell, Runtime: Phase 3: Runtime Discovery & Heartbeat
    Shell->>RegAPI: GET /api/apps (Discover registered apps)
    RegAPI-->>Shell: Return app federation manifest
    Shell->>RefApp: Mount remote module / render route
    Runtime->>RefApp: GET /health (Heartbeat probe)
    RefApp-->>Runtime: 200 OK { status: "healthy" }
```

---

## 2. Step-by-Step Developer Walkthrough

### Step 1: Create a Minimal Standalone App

Initialize a tiny React application using Vite:

```bash
npm create vite@latest reference-widget -- --template react-ts
cd reference-widget
npm install
```

### Step 2: Implement the Health Endpoint & Registration Metadata

In your app, expose a standard health check and metadata descriptor so the FuzeFront runtime can monitor it. Create `src/fuze-metadata.ts`:

```typescript
export const fuzeAppMetadata = {
  id: "reference-widget",
  name: "Reference Widget",
  version: "1.0.0",
  entryPoint: "/assets/remoteEntry.js",
  routes: [
    { path: "/widget", component: "WidgetRoot" }
  ],
  healthCheckUrl: "/health"
};

export function handleHealthCheck(req: any, res: any) {
  res.status(200).json({
    status: "healthy",
    app: fuzeAppMetadata.id,
    timestamp: new Date().toISOString()
  });
}
```

### Step 3: Registration Contract & Required Payload

To register the application with FuzeFront's Applications Service, send the registration contract payload:

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3001/api/apps \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer <YOUR_DEVELOPER_TOKEN>" \
  -d '{
    "id": "reference-widget",
    "name": "Reference Widget",
    "version": "1.0.0",
    "baseUrl": "http://localhost:5173",
    "metadata": {
      "entryPoint": "/src/main.tsx",
      "healthEndpoint": "/health"
    }
  }'
```

Expected response:
```json
{
  "success": true,
  "app": {
    "id": "reference-widget",
    "status": "registered",
    "registeredAt": "2026-03-30T12:00:00.000Z"
  }
}
```

---

## 3. Auth, Routing & Health Assumptions

- **Authentication:** FuzeFront injects the active tenant context and user session claims via HTTP headers (`X-Fuze-Tenant-Id`, `X-Fuze-User-Id`) or session cookies. Standalone apps must validate these tokens against the FuzeFront security broker (`/api/auth/verify`).
- **Routing:** Apps are mounted dynamically under the host shell using Module Federation or iframe isolation. Relative paths must respect the assigned prefix (e.g., `/apps/reference-widget/*`).
- **Heartbeat:** The runtime health monitor pings the app's `healthEndpoint` every 30 seconds. Consecutive failures transition the app state from `healthy` to `degraded` or `offline` in the host registry.

---

## 4. Documented Friction & Realistic Failure Modes

When onboarding existing apps, developers typically encounter the following friction points:

1. **CORS and Origin Mismatch:**
   * *Symptom:* Host shell fails to load remote assets, throwing CORS policy errors.
   * *Troubleshooting:* Ensure your Vite dev server or production container correctly sets `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` or explicitly allows the FuzeFront host domain.
2. **Missing Registration Metadata / 401 Unauthorized:**
   * *Symptom:* `POST /api/apps` returns `401 Unauthorized` or `400 Bad Request`.
   * *Troubleshooting:* Verify that your developer bearer token has `apps:write` permissions and that all required fields (`id`, `name`, `baseUrl`) are present in the JSON payload.
3. **Health Probe Timeout:**
   * *Symptom:* App registers successfully but flips to `offline` within a minute.
   * *Troubleshooting:* Check that your `/health` endpoint responds within 2 seconds, does not block on heavy database migrations during startup, and correctly listens on the expected network interface/port.

--- deploy/helm/fuzefront/values-prod.yaml ---
# =============================================================================
# Production overlay (Contabo k3s), consumed by the Argo CD `fuzefront` Application.
# Differs from local by: GHCR images, public host + TLS, sealed secret, prod
# Authentik OIDC, Prometheus metrics, pre-created Kafka topics, and node-2
# placement for heavy stateless services.
#
# Node topology (see docs/deployment/CONTABO_DEPLOYMENT.md):
#   node-1 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-1): control-plane + stateful
#           (FuzeInfra Postgres/Redis/Kafka/Chroma live here on local-path).
#   node-2 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-2): heavy stateless compute
#           (litellm/chat/billing). Relabel/rename to match the real join.
# All secrets come from the SealedSecret `fuzefront-secrets` — never inline here.
# =============================================================================
global:
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  # Default placement: none (let the scheduler spread app pods across both nodes).
  # Heavy stateless services pin to node-2 via their own affinity blocks below.
  scheduling:
    nodeSelector: {}
    affinity: {}
    # Tolerate FuzeInfra's durable-node taint.
    #
    # FuzeInfra is tainting its three durable (control-plane/etcd) nodes
    # `fuzeinfra.io/durable=true:NoSchedule` so that application workloads stop
    # landing on them. Measured there on 2026-09-07: 70 and 57 pods on two of the
    # three, 20,585 container restarts, load average 59, and etcd losing
    # heartbeats on the node that was also the raft leader.
    #
    # FuzeFront is explicitly IN SCOPE for those nodes -- it is platform frontend,
    # not a tenant app -- so it must carry the toleration or it gets pushed onto
    # the autoscaled elastic pool, which is reaped on billing boundaries.
    #
    # THIS WILL NOT LOOK BROKEN IF IT IS MISSING. NoSchedule does not evict, so
    # when the taint lands every FuzeFront pod keeps running exactly as before.
    # It breaks at the NEXT restart or rollout, when those pods can no longer be
    # placed back -- a delayed failure that reads as unrelated to the taint. That
    # is why this has to land BEFORE the taint, not after it.
    #
    # TOLERATION IS NOT PLACEMENT. This only makes the durable nodes *eligible*;
    # the scheduler may still choose elastic. Moving specific backend services
    # deliberately ONTO elastic is a separate concern, expressed per-service via
    # nodeSelector/affinity (see PR #910) -- and note the `fuzefront.scheduling`
    # helper resolves per-service over global, so a service that declares its own
    # `tolerations` REPLACES this list rather than adding to it. A service pinned
    # to elastic simply does not need it.
    #
    # Tracked in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#913; the matching FuzeInfra-side tolerations
    # (longhorn, coredns, ARC controller, Argo CD) landed in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#921.
    tolerations:
      - key: fuzeinfra.io/durable
        operator: Equal
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule

# Prometheus scrape annotations on FuzeFront pods. The FuzeInfra Prometheus
# auto-discovers pods carrying prometheus.io/scrape=true (see Phase E). The
# backend exposes /metrics via prom-client; other pods are annotated for when
# their /metrics lands.
observability:
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    path: /metrics

# Fleet policy: only core infra + frontend services stay on the durable/
# control-plane node pool (vmi3383846/vmi3396106); backend/worker pods for an
# individual product move to the autoscaled `elastic` pool instead. Every
# service below reaches its state (Postgres/Redis/Mongo/Kafka) over the
# network in the `fuzeinfra` namespace, not via a local PVC, so this is a
# plain placement change — mirrors FuzeInfra's
# runners/arc/runner-scale-set-values.yaml pattern. `frontend` below is
# deliberately NOT given this block; it is the one service this policy keeps
# on durable.
.elasticPlacement: &elasticPlacement
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: fuzeinfra.io/pool
                operator: In
                values:
                  - elastic
  tolerations:
    - key: fuzeinfra.io/elastic
      operator: Exists
      effect: PreferNoSchedule

# FuzeFront Adoption Quickstart

This guide is for developers and teams evaluating FuzeFront as a real platform component rather than just reading about the architecture.

## Pick your path

### 0. Reference Application Onboarding (New!)
Want to see how a tiny standalone React/Vite app is registered, authenticated, routed, and health-monitored in FuzeFront? 
Read our complete step-by-step guide: [Reference App Onboarding Walkthrough](./guides/reference-app-onboarding.md).

### 1. Developer: run the platform locally

```bash
npm run install:all
npm run db:init
npm run db:seed
npm run demo
```

Then inspect the runtime app registry, the example federated application, health updates, routing, and the integration SDK.

### 2. Platform engineer: run the Kubernetes path

```bash
cd FuzeInfra && make kind-up && cd ..

docker build -t fuzefront/backend:local ./backend
docker build -t fuzefront/frontend:local \
  --build-arg VITE_API_URL=http://fuzefront.dev.local ./frontend

kind load docker-image \
  fuzefront/backend:local \
  fuzefront/frontend:local \
  --name fuzeinfra

helm upgrade --install fuzefront deploy/helm/fuzefront \
  -n fuzefront --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/helm/fuzefront/values-local.yaml
```

### 3. Architecture reviewer: challenge the design

Read `docs/SOFTWARE_FACTORY.md`, then join the public architecture review:

https://github.com/izzywdev/FuzeFront/issues/1015

We specifically want concrete failure modes, security concerns, coupling problems, operational risks, and examples where an existing platform solves the problem better.

### 4. Design partner: bring a real workload

Open a Design Partner issue or start from:

https://github.com/izzywdev/FuzeFront/issues/1016

Useful evaluation cases include:

- a startup operating several products with a small team;

# =============================================================================
# Production overlay (Contabo k3s), consumed by the Argo CD `fuzefront` Application.
# Differs from local by: GHCR images, public host + TLS, sealed secret, prod
# Authentik OIDC, Prometheus metrics, pre-created Kafka topics, and node-2
# placement for heavy stateless services.
#
# Node topology (see docs/deployment/CONTABO_DEPLOYMENT.md):
#   node-1 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-1): control-plane + stateful
#           (FuzeInfra Postgres/Redis/Kafka/Chroma live here on local-path).
#   node-2 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-2): heavy stateless compute
#           (litellm/chat/billing). Relabel/rename to match the real join.
# All secrets come from the SealedSecret `fuzefront-secrets` — never inline here.
# =============================================================================
global:
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  # Default placement: none (let the scheduler spread app pods across both nodes).
  # Heavy stateless services pin to node-2 via their own affinity blocks below.
  scheduling:
    nodeSelector: {}
    affinity: {}
    # Tolerate FuzeInfra's durable-node taint.
    #
    # FuzeInfra is tainting its three durable (control-plane/etcd) nodes
    # `fuzeinfra.io/durable=true:NoSchedule` so that application workloads stop
    # landing on them. Measured there on 2026-09-07: 70 and 57 pods on two of the
    # three, 20,585 container restarts, load average 59, and etcd losing
    # heartbeats on the node that was also the raft leader.
    #
    # FuzeFront is explicitly IN SCOPE for those nodes -- it is platform frontend,
    # not a tenant app -- so it must carry the toleration or it gets pushed onto
    # the autoscaled elastic pool, which is reaped on billing boundaries.
    #
    # THIS WILL NOT LOOK BROKEN IF IT IS MISSING. NoSchedule does not evict, so
    # when the taint lands every FuzeFront pod keeps running exactly as before.
    # It breaks at the NEXT restart or rollout, when those pods can no longer be
    # placed back -- a delayed failure that reads as unrelated to the taint. That
    # is why this has to land BEFORE the taint, not after it.
    #
    # TOLERATION IS NOT PLACEMENT. This only makes the durable nodes *eligible*;
    # the scheduler may still choose elastic. Moving specific backend services
    # deliberately ONTO elastic is a separate concern, expressed per-service via
    # nodeSelector/affinity (see PR #910) -- and note the `fuzefront.scheduling`
    # helper resolves per-service over global, so a service that declares its own
    # `tolerations` REPLACES this list rather than adding to it. A service pinned
    # to elastic simply does not need it.
    #
    # Tracked in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#913; the matching FuzeInfra-side tolerations
    # (longhorn, coredns, ARC controller, Argo CD) landed in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#921.
    tolerations:
      - key: fuzeinfra.io/durable
        operator: Equal
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule

# Prometheus scrape annotations on FuzeFront pods. The FuzeInfra Prometheus
# auto-discovers pods carrying prometheus.io/scrape=true (see Phase E). The
# backend exposes /metrics via prom-client; other pods are annotated for when
# their /metrics lands.
observability:
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    path: /metrics

# Fleet policy: only core infra + frontend services stay on the durable/
# control-plane node pool (vmi3383846/vmi3396106); backend/worker pods for an
# individual product move to the autoscaled `elastic` pool instead. Every
# service below reaches its state (Postgres/Redis/Mongo/Kafka) over the
# network in the `fuzeinfra` namespace, not via a local PVC, so this is a
# plain placement change — mirrors FuzeInfra's
# runners/arc/runner-scale-set-values.yaml pattern. `frontend` below is
# deliberately NOT given this block; it is the one service this policy keeps
# on durable.
.elasticPlacement: &elasticPlacement
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: fuzeinfra.io/pool
                operator: In
                values:
                  - elastic
  tolerations:
    - key: fuzeinfra.io/elastic
      operator: Exists
      effect: PreferNoSchedule

# FuzeFront Adoption Quickstart

This guide is for developers and teams evaluating FuzeFront as a real platform component rather than just reading about the architecture.

## Pick your path

### 1. Developer: run the platform locally

```bash
npm run install:all
npm run db:init
npm run db:seed
npm run demo
```

Then inspect the runtime app registry, the example federated application, health updates, routing, and the integration SDK.

### 2. Platform engineer: run the Kubernetes path

```bash
cd FuzeInfra && make kind-up && cd ..

docker build -t fuzefront/backend:local ./backend
docker build -t fuzefront/frontend:local \
  --build-arg VITE_API_URL=http://fuzefront.dev.local ./frontend

kind load docker-image \
  fuzefront/backend:local \
  fuzefront/frontend:local \
  --name fuzeinfra

helm upgrade --install fuzefront deploy/helm/fuzefront \
  -n fuzefront --create-namespace \
  -f deploy/helm/fuzefront/values-local.yaml
```

### 3. Architecture reviewer: challenge the design

Read `docs/SOFTWARE_FACTORY.md`, then join the public architecture review:

https://github.com/izzywdev/FuzeFront/issues/1015

We specifically want concrete failure modes, security concerns, coupling problems, operational risks, and examples where an existing platform solves the problem better.

### 4. Design partner: bring a real workload

Open a Design Partner issue or start from:

https://github.com/izzywdev/FuzeFront/issues/1016

Useful evaluation cases include:

- a startup operating several products with a small team;
- a platform team standardizing app delivery;
- a software studio repeatedly rebuilding common infrastructure;
- a CTO testing governed AI-assisted delivery;
- an independent founder trying to maximize organizational leverage.

## What success looks like

For each real evaluation we want to capture:

- time to first successful local run;
- time to onboard an existing app;
- what manual work was eliminated;
- what still required custom integration;
- where the abstractions leaked;
- deployment and operational friction;
- security or governance concerns;
- whether a second application becomes materially easier than the first.

## Contribute

Look for issues labeled `good first issue`, `help wanted`, `community`, or `adoption`.

Small fixes are welcome. Documentation, examples, integration adapters, developer-experience improvements, tests, reproducible bug reports, and architecture criticism are all useful contributions.

See `COMMUNITY.md` and `CONTRIBUTING.md` for the broader participation model.

--- deploy/helm/fuzefront/values-prod.yaml ---
# =============================================================================
# Production overlay (Contabo k3s), consumed by the Argo CD `fuzefront` Application.
# Differs from local by: GHCR images, public host + TLS, sealed secret, prod
# Authentik OIDC, Prometheus metrics, pre-created Kafka topics, and node-2
# placement for heavy stateless services.
#
# Node topology (see docs/deployment/CONTABO_DEPLOYMENT.md):
#   node-1 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-1): control-plane + stateful
#           (FuzeInfra Postgres/Redis/Kafka/Chroma live here on local-path).
#   node-2 (kubernetes.io/hostname=fuzefront-node-2): heavy stateless compute
#           (litellm/chat/billing). Relabel/rename to match the real join.
# All secrets come from the SealedSecret `fuzefront-secrets` — never inline here.
# =============================================================================
global:
  imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
  # Default placement: none (let the scheduler spread app pods across both nodes).
  # Heavy stateless services pin to node-2 via their own affinity blocks below.
  scheduling:
    nodeSelector: {}
    affinity: {}
    # Tolerate FuzeInfra's durable-node taint.
    #
    # FuzeInfra is tainting its three durable (control-plane/etcd) nodes
    # `fuzeinfra.io/durable=true:NoSchedule` so that application workloads stop
    # landing on them. Measured there on 2026-09-07: 70 and 57 pods on two of the
    # three, 20,585 container restarts, load average 59, and etcd losing
    # heartbeats on the node that was also the raft leader.
    #
    # FuzeFront is explicitly IN SCOPE for those nodes -- it is platform frontend,
    # not a tenant app -- so it must carry the toleration or it gets pushed onto
    # the autoscaled elastic pool, which is reaped on billing boundaries.
    #
    # THIS WILL NOT LOOK BROKEN IF IT IS MISSING. NoSchedule does not evict, so
    # when the taint lands every FuzeFront pod keeps running exactly as before.
    # It breaks at the NEXT restart or rollout, when those pods can no longer be
    # placed back -- a delayed failure that reads as unrelated to the taint. That
    # is why this has to land BEFORE the taint, not after it.
    #
    # TOLERATION IS NOT PLACEMENT. This only makes the durable nodes *eligible*;
    # the scheduler may still choose elastic. Moving specific backend services
    # deliberately ONTO elastic is a separate concern, expressed per-service via
    # nodeSelector/affinity (see PR #910) -- and note the `fuzefront.scheduling`
    # helper resolves per-service over global, so a service that declares its own
    # `tolerations` REPLACES this list rather than adding to it. A service pinned
    # to elastic simply does not need it.
    #
    # Tracked in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#913; the matching FuzeInfra-side tolerations
    # (longhorn, coredns, ARC controller, Argo CD) landed in izzywdev/FuzeInfra#921.
    tolerations:
      - key: fuzeinfra.io/durable
        operator: Equal
        value: "true"
        effect: NoSchedule

# Prometheus scrape annotations on FuzeFront pods. The FuzeInfra Prometheus
# auto-discovers pods carrying prometheus.io/scrape=true (see Phase E). The
# backend exposes /metrics via prom-client; other pods are annotated for when
# their /metrics lands.
observability:
  metrics:
    enabled: true
    path: /metrics

# Fleet policy: only core infra + frontend services stay on the durable/
# control-plane node pool (vmi3383846/vmi3396106); backend/worker pods for an
# individual product move to the autoscaled `elastic` pool instead. Every
# service below reaches its state (Postgres/Redis/Mongo/Kafka) over the
# network in the `fuzeinfra` namespace, not via a local PVC, so this is a
# plain placement change — mirrors FuzeInfra's
# runners/arc/runner-scale-set-values.yaml pattern. `frontend` below is
# deliberately NOT given this block; it is the one service this policy keeps
# on durable.
.elasticPlacement: &elasticPlacement
  affinity:
    nodeAffinity:
      requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
        nodeSelectorTerms:
          - matchExpressions:
              - key: fuzeinfra.io/pool
                operator: In
                values:
                  - elastic
  tolerations:
    - key: fuzeinfra.io/elastic
      operator: Exists
      effect: PreferNoSchedule
